grounds.point: The Rent Control Tribunal and the High Court found against the tenant on whether it had sub-let or parted with possession in favour of R.C. Abrol & Company Pvt. Ltd.
grounds.explanation: The allowed record expressly states that the Tribunal found against the tenant on this contention and that the High Court affirmed those findings. Section 14(1)(b) reaches sub-letting, assignment, or otherwise parting with possession, so this preserved prior finding supplies the transfer-of-possession component of the fixed ground.

grounds.point: Clause 14 permitted R.C. Abrol & Co. to share the premises with the lessor's permission.
grounds.explanation: The written lease states both that the lessee would not sub-let without the lessor's written permission and that its contractors R.C. Abrol & Co. would share the premises with the lessor's permission. This is significant written evidence of permission to share, but the supplied record does not establish that the permission extended to the sub-letting or parting with possession that the Tribunal and High Court found.

grounds.point: The tenant's contention that any actionable sub-letting had the landlord's written consent was rejected by the Tribunal and affirmed by the High Court.
grounds.explanation: The allowed record preserves the tenant's written-consent contention and expressly says the Tribunal found against it, with the High Court affirming. Because section 14(1)(b) conditions this eviction ground on the relevant sub-letting, assignment, or parting with possession occurring without the landlord's written consent, that prior finding supports the statutory absence-of-written-consent element despite Clause 14's narrower permission to share.

grounds.point: Under the supplied Delhi provision, post-9 June 1952 sub-letting, assignment, or other parting with possession without written landlord consent is an eviction ground.
grounds.explanation: Section 14(1)(b) expressly supplies this ground, and section 16 likewise requires written consent for relevant post-1952 sub-letting and, after commencement of the Act, for transfer or assignment of tenancy rights. The supplied statutory reproduction therefore makes written consent a substantive condition within the fixed ground.

grounds.point: The supplied precedent describes Delhi section 14(b) as broad enough to include sublease, assignment, other modes of parting with possession, and even involuntary sale.
grounds.explanation: General Radio reports Parasaram as construing the Delhi provision broadly in a liquidation-sale setting. Its status is only a reported precedent rather than the independently supplied Parasaram opinion, but it supports a broad understanding of the statutory transfer language and does not supply an exception applicable to the preserved finding involving R.C. Abrol & Company.

grounds.point: The supplied Telesound passage does not establish a general exception from section 14(1)(b) for transfers said to occur with legal or court-related authorization.
grounds.explanation: Telesound expressed only a prima facie view concerning amalgamation and expressly reserved whether the resulting transfer would constitute an assignment attracting section 14(1)(b), leaving the landlord free to pursue that question before the proper authority. It therefore does not displace the Delhi statutory rule or the preserved target findings here.

reason: The allowed record preserves affirmed findings that the tenant sub-let or parted with possession in favour of R.C. Abrol & Company Pvt. Ltd. and that its written-consent defense failed. Given section 14(1)(b)'s express requirement of written landlord consent and the absence of any supplied controlling exception that defeats those findings, the fixed eviction ground is supported.
